dimensions.description: Needs clear goals, expectations, and success criteria — including quality bar, definition of done, and what matters most right now — made clear up front, before committing to action

Treats written documentation — summaries, notes, decisions, a kept-up-to-date plan — as the reliable source of truth for alignment; prefers important things written down and easy to return to, rather than living only in conversation or memory

Gets context best from real examples — code, tickets, past work, existing standards — rather than abstract descriptions; trusts the actual work as the clearest guide, and likes context to live next to what it describes

Prefers live conversation over writing — for aligning, understanding, and working things out; values real-time back-and-forth, where you can test understanding, read tone, and ask follow-up questions, over written exchange
Figures things out by trying something real — starting small, exploring, and learning through progress — rather than by reading or discussing about it first
Comfortable moving forward with incomplete information or undefined constraints; does not need everything pinned down to start, and is at ease refining as things become clearer

Needs clear definition of who owns which decisions and responsibilities — including where their own judgment and authority apply; unclear ownership leads to duplication, dropped work, and confusion over who to go to

Values work being visible as it happens — seeing others' progress, blockers, and state, and keeping their own work open rather than hidden until it is finished; prefers a live view and transparency over periodic summaries or working out of sight
Needs to understand team norms, roles, and interpersonal context — whether to integrate into a new team or to make well-informed decisions about situations involving multiple people
Needs explicit shared agreement before acting — checks understanding rather than running on unspoken assumptions, and wants the people affected genuinely on board first
Expects risks, gaps, and problems — including in their own work — to be surfaced early and openly rather than held back; would rather raise something uncertain than let it become a surprise
Prefers alignment and updates at predictable, structured moments rather than continuously; values a regular rhythm people can prepare for, sometimes for the consistency itself
Values protecting uninterrupted work time; sensitive to interruptions, unnecessary meetings, and context switching that pull focus without enough payoff
Prefers addressing misalignment, blockers, or issues as soon as they appear rather than waiting for a better moment; would rather raise or resolve something now than let it sit
Prefers fixed delivery cycles (like sprints) with dedicated moments to plan, review, and reflect; a predictable cadence helps them work well
Prefers continuous work pulled from a prioritized backlog, without fixed cycles or waiting for the next one to start; plans just enough to begin and lets the rest emerge
Prefers clarifying full scope, dependencies, milestones, and risks before beginning execution; wants the whole picture mapped out to move confidently
Prefers starting with a rough direction and refining the plan progressively as work progresses and more is learned, rather than committing to a full plan up front

Prefers grounding plans in small experiments or observable signals before committing to a direction — would rather test an assumption than commit to it untested, especially when uncertainty or risk is high
Expects to be involved in decisions that affect their work before they are finalized — wants a genuine say and a chance to weigh in, not just to be informed after the fact
Expects changes to be batched into planning points rather than introduced mid-flow; protects work in progress from a constant stream of reprioritization
Expects new work to require an explicit trade-off against existing commitments — if something is added, something else should be dropped or deprioritized, not piled on top
Values a sustainable workload and resists scope or pace inflation; protective of not overcommitting or burning out
Expects trade-offs, alternatives considered, and what is being given up to be made explicit
Comfortable accepting scope or plan changes without needing extensive process or justification; values being able to respond to something important without friction
Considers work done when the core problem is solved reliably; treats follow-up items as not always a gate, and values steady progress over waiting for perfect
Needs a peer review or external check before fully trusting a handoff or considering work complete; another set of eyes is what makes the work feel sound
Prefers assessing severity, actual impact, and the full picture before reacting; values proportionate, considered responses over immediate alarm

Prefers resolving problems independently before involving others; when in a leading role, encourages direct resolution between parties first before intervening — avoids creating unnecessary noise or dependency
Prioritizes understanding why a problem happened — looking at patterns and root causes, not just the surface fix — to prevent it recurring
Protects the quality bar even under deadline pressure; treats some quality risks as non-negotiable, even if it means pushing back on scope or timeline
Prioritizes owning and fixing a problem over explaining or questioning it; when something goes wrong, the instinct is to take responsibility and repair rather than justify
Validates whether a concern reflects a real gap before accepting it; does not treat every finding as a problem by default, and examines the concern itself before acting on it
When giving feedback, prioritizes accuracy and substance over delivery style; believes valid concerns should not be dismissed due to discomfort
When giving feedback, believes delivery style is essential to effectiveness; adjusts how feedback is given so the other person can actually use it
When receiving feedback, extracts useful signal even from poor delivery; does not let style get in the way of hearing the concern
When receiving feedback, needs delivery to be appropriate before being able to process the concern; style affects ability to engage
Prefers to explicitly agree on shared norms for how concerns, feedback, and tension are handled — fixing the pattern, not just resolving the immediate instance
Prefers to raise concerns privately first; treats public discussion of problems as a last resort
Needs public feedback to be handled respectfully and without embarrassment; dignity is a precondition for engagement
Needs repair after a difficult or public exchange — often a private follow-up conversation — so the relationship stays intact, separately from resolving the issue itself
Expects to manage their own work tempo and rhythm without regular monitoring; frequent purposeless check-ins feel like distrust

Expects to decide how to execute the work they own, and to make trade-offs within that scope without seeking approval for every step; detailed direction on owned work feels like a lack of trust in their judgment
Accepts oversight when it comes from a place of support; rejects oversight that feels driven by anxiety, distrust, or a need to approve every step
Needs access to guidance or decision help when blocked; unavailable support on important decisions feels like abandonment
Needs ongoing calibrating signals, feedback, and encouragement — not just to hear something when it goes wrong; values genuine two-way exchange over working in silence
When blocked or unsure, prefers a concrete decision or recommendation over collaborative exploration; wants to be unblocked, not facilitated
Needs to be able to ask for support without it being interpreted as a lack of competence; psychological safety to seek help is part of healthy ownership

Needs time and effort — whether a meeting, a difficult conversation, or a solo workday — to produce something concrete and visible: a decision, next step, resolution, or real progress; effort without a tangible result is hard to justify
Values regular human connection and team cohesion beyond just getting tasks done; familiarity, rhythm, and the relationships themselves matter independently of output
Needs urgency communicated calmly and factually; does not want stress, anxiety, or pressure to be performed — clarity over dramatisation
Galvanized by high-pressure, consequence-laden, or accountability-based urgency communication; responds to stress-driven framing
Motivated by positive, encouraging, and purpose-driven framing; responds to excitement and support rather than pressure or consequences
Self-motivated and does not need external motivational input; finds speeches or pep talks distracting rather than helpful, and draws drive from within rather than from others
Addresses interpersonal friction directly with the person involved, even when uncomfortable; prefers to name and work through things early rather than avoid them or route around them
Genuinely absorbs uncomfortable communication styles without needing to address them; personal discomfort is not sufficient reason to escalate
Uses team impact rather than personal discomfort as the threshold for action; what matters is the effect on the team and the work, not how something feels personally
Avoids direct confrontation of uncomfortable patterns; needs distance and processing time before deciding whether to act
Processes interpersonal friction by naming it to a trusted third party rather than raising it directly with the person involved
Believes interpersonal tension needs time and space to settle before a direct conversation can be productive; engaging while tension is still active tends to produce reactions rather than resolution
Readily involves higher authority when a problem exceeds what the direct parties can resolve; treats escalation as a legitimate and timely tool rather than a last resort
In difficult conversations, prioritizes both perspectives being genuinely heard over reaching a concrete outcome or agreement; needs acknowledgment before being able to move on

In difficult conversations, expects both parties to acknowledge their part rather than one person identifying the problem and the other owning the fix — for example, if a deadline was missed, both the person who missed it and the person who set unclear expectations should own something

Views structured facilitation as a legitimate tool for resolving conflict — whether as a participant open to third-party help, or as a leader actively stepping in to bring conflicting parties together in a structured way

Believes conflict resolves more reliably when a team builds deliberate habits — such as retrospectives that include interpersonal health, explicit norms for raising concerns, or regular check-ins where naming tension is normalized — rather than relying on ad-hoc intervention after something breaks
Motivated primarily by the quality and difficulty of the work itself; finds genuine satisfaction in building things well and solving hard problems, independent of external recognition or purpose
Needs to understand why work matters and how it connects to a meaningful outcome; motivation drops significantly when work feels disconnected from purpose or when the reason behind a task is unclear
Motivated primarily by being given real ownership and the freedom to make decisions; without genuine trust and responsibility, work loses its meaning
Motivated primarily by the people, team, and shared experience of building something together; relationships matter more as a source of drive than the work itself
Values being seen and acknowledged during difficult or pressured periods more than routine praise; recognition when things are hard feels more meaningful than being praised when things are easy
Finds a workday worthwhile when understanding of the problem, system, or people has genuinely improved; values insight and better mental models as an end in themselves, even without visible output
Believes process, planning, and delivery reliability are important enough to examine as a team; considers operational execution the core topic for retrospectives
Believes technical quality, incidents, and maintainability deserve regular team reflection; considers soundness as important as delivery speed
Believes collaboration patterns and communication habits are worth examining as a team, even when they feel less urgent than delivery; expects friction here to eventually show up in the work
Believes team safety, pressure, and how people are treated are foundational reflection topics; thinks problems hidden by unsafe culture are the hardest to fix later

Finds quiet satisfaction in leaving things better than they were found — cleaner code, clearer process, a resolved disagreement; enjoys small steady improvements for their own sake, without needing recognition or a big visible result
